articles.title: Writing on the Back of the Photograph
articles.dek: An old fisherman, close to death, picks up a pen to make sure the brightest day of his life is never forgotten. The words he chose show that he never stopped thinking about that mountain.
articles.quote: The glory Peter once tried to keep in tents on a hilltop, he finally carried down the mountain in words his friends could keep.
articles.body:
In many Filipino homes there is a box that nobody throws away. It might be an old shoebox from a Christmas long ago, or a blue tin that once held butter cookies and has not held a cookie in thirty years. Inside are photographs: a wedding in a provincial church with the bride squinting into the sun, a baby propped on a capiz table, young men in stiff barong standing in front of a brand-new jeepney. For years the box sits on top of the aparador, until one rainy afternoon a grandchild pulls it down, holds up a faded picture, and asks, "La, sino po ito?"

What happens next is one of the loveliest scenes in family life. Lola puts on her reading glasses, finds a ballpen, and starts writing on the backs of the pictures. "Tito Ben, Bauang, 1968." "Your Lolo, the day he came home from Saudi." "Me, pregnant with your mama, the year of the big typhoon." She takes her time and presses hard so the ink will last, because she understands something the grandchild has not yet considered. A day is coming when no one in the house will be able to answer the question, and a face without a name slowly becomes a stranger. So while she still can, she writes the stories where they will outlive her.

Nearly two thousand years ago, an old fisherman did the same thing. Christian tradition, early and widespread, places Simon Peter in Rome in the mid-60s AD, during the reign of Nero, when following Jesus had become a dangerous thing to do. The hands that once hauled dripping nets on the Sea of Galilee were now spotted with age. He had not forgotten what Jesus told him on a beach after the resurrection: "when you are old you will stretch out your hands, and someone else will dress you and lead you where you do not want to go" (John 21:18). John adds that Jesus said this "to indicate the kind of death by which Peter would glorify God" (John 21:19). Decades later, Peter could feel that day approaching.

He also knew that the churches he loved were under pressure from a quieter danger. Smooth-talking teachers had begun to appear among them (2 Peter 2:1), and scoffers were asking, "Where is this 'coming' he promised?" (2 Peter 3:4). Their suggestion was simple and corrosive: perhaps the whole story about Jesus was a pious legend, a beautiful tale that grew in the retelling. So the old apostle picked up his pen to write what would be his last letter, and as he wrote, his mind went back to the brightest day of his life.

It had happened on a high mountain. Jesus took Peter, James and John up the slopes with him, and there, in front of them, "his face shone like the sun, and his clothes became as white as the light" (Matthew 17:2). Moses and Elijah appeared and spoke with him. Peter, who always talked when he was nervous, blurted out a plan: "Lord, it is good for us to be here. If you wish, I will put up three shelters" (Matthew 17:4). Mark, who many believe wrote down Peter's own preaching, adds an honest little line: "He did not know what to say, they were so frightened" (Mark 9:6). Then a bright cloud swallowed them, and a voice spoke out of it, and the three fishermen fell face down on the ground.

Now, as an old man, Peter writes:

"I think it is right to refresh your memory as long as I live in the tent of this body, because I know that I will soon put it aside, as our Lord Jesus Christ has made clear to me. And I will make every effort to see that after my departure you will always be able to remember these things." (2 Peter 1:13–15)

Two small words in that passage open a window into Peter's heart. The first is "tent." The Greek word is skēnōma, a dwelling made of cloth, the kind of thing you fold up and carry away. It belongs to the same family as skēnē, the word Matthew uses for the "shelters" Peter offered to build on the mountain. The second word is "departure." Peter's Greek word is exodos, the word we know as "exodus," the name for Israel's long walk out of slavery toward the promised land. Luke, telling the story of that same mountain, records what Moses and Elijah were discussing with Jesus: "They spoke about his departure, which he was about to bring to fulfillment at Jerusalem" (Luke 9:31). The word there is the same, exodos.

One way to read this is that Peter, writing about his own death, is still standing on that mountain in his mind. As a young man he wanted to pitch tents and stay forever in the glow. As an old man he calls his own body a tent, and he uses for his own death the very word that had been spoken about his Master's. He has come to see his death as an exodus, a departure that follows the path Jesus walked before him. And he has learned that the glory of that day could never be kept in shelters on a hilltop. The glory Peter once tried to keep in tents on a hilltop, he finally carried down the mountain in words his friends could keep.

That is why he speaks so carefully in the lines that follow. "For we did not follow cleverly devised stories when we told you about the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ in power, but we were eyewitnesses of his majesty" (2 Peter 1:16). The phrase "cleverly devised stories" translates the Greek mythoi, the word from which we get "myths," and Peter sets it plainly against what he saw with his own eyes. Then he adds a detail that sounds like an old man pointing at a photograph: "We ourselves heard this voice that came from heaven when we were with him on the sacred mountain" (2 Peter 1:18). He is writing a name and a place on the back of the picture, so that no one can later say the face belongs to a stranger.

There is real comfort in verse 12, which is easy to read past. Peter says he will keep reminding his readers "even though you know them and are firmly established in the truth you now have" (2 Peter 1:12). He does not scold them for forgetting. He simply assumes that people who know the truth still need to hear it again, the way ink on the back of an old photo needs to be traced over before it fades. Faith works this way for most of us. We do remember that God has been good, and yet on a hard Tuesday, with the bills on the table and the hospital results not back yet, that memory can feel faint and far away. The word Peter uses for "refresh" carries the sense of waking someone up thoroughly, and sometimes the soul needs that kind of gentle shaking.

Each of us has our own small box of mountain moments. Perhaps it is the night a sick child's fever finally broke, or the job offer that arrived the week the money ran out, or the quiet morning when a verse you had read a hundred times suddenly spoke straight to your grief. These moments are precious, and they are also fragile, because unlabeled memories blur with time. Peter's example invites us to do what Lola does with her ballpen: to write down, while we still can, the name and the date and the place where God showed himself faithful.

You might do it tonight in a simple way. Take a notebook, or open the notes app on your phone, and write down one specific time the Lord came through for you, with the year, the place, and the names of the people who were there. Then, sometime this week, tell that story to someone younger, perhaps over merienda or during the long ride home, the way our families have always passed things down through kuwentuhan around the table. You will be doing exactly what Peter did in his last letter, making sure that after you are gone, someone will still be able to remember.

Peter's letter is, in a sense, a labeled photograph that has survived twenty centuries. On the back, in an old fisherman's hand, it still reads: the sacred mountain, we ourselves heard. Because he took the time to write it down, you and I can hold that picture today and know whose face is shining in it. May the Lord give you the grace to label your own pictures well, so that the faces of his faithfulness are never strangers to the ones who come after you.

articles.title: The Table at the Heart of the House
articles.dek: Ezekiel's guide measured walls and doorways for chapters, but spoke only twice inside the temple itself. The second time, he pointed to a piece of wooden furniture and called it a table.
articles.quote: In the heart of God's house, the furniture is arranged for company.
articles.body:
In the hungry winter of 1933, a journalist named Dorothy Day began handing out a newspaper on the streets of New York for a penny a copy. The Great Depression had emptied factories and filled sidewalks, and before long the people reading her paper started knocking on her door. She and her friend Peter Maurin opened what they called houses of hospitality, plain rented rooms where anyone could come in out of the cold, take a bowl of soup and a slice of bread, and sit down. Day insisted on that last part. She wanted the guests seated at tables, and she wanted the workers sitting among them, eating the same food from the same pot, so that nobody who walked in would feel like a case being processed.

Years later, in the closing pages of her autobiography The Long Loneliness, she tried to explain what all those crowded meals had taught her. "We cannot love God unless we love each other, and to love we must know each other," she wrote. "We know Him in the breaking of bread, and we know each other in the breaking of bread, and we are not alone any more." She had discovered something very old, the same truth tucked into one quiet verse of Ezekiel that most readers rush past on the way to somewhere more exciting.

Ezekiel 40 to 42 can feel like reading a blueprint aloud. A man whose appearance shines like bronze leads the prophet through a vast temple with a measuring rod in his hand, and the text records nearly every step: gateways, porches, side rooms, thresholds, thicknesses of walls, cubit after cubit after cubit. It is easy to lose heart in the numbers. Yet the setting makes these chapters some of the most tender in the book. Ezekiel was a priest (Ezekiel 1:3) living as an exile in Babylon, and the vision came "in the twenty-fifth year of our exile" and "in the fourteenth year after the fall of the city" (Ezekiel 40:1). Solomon's temple was ash. The priest had no altar to serve at, and his people had no house of God to go home to.

So God gave him a house to walk through, measured with care, as if to say that nothing about his dwelling with his people had been forgotten. In chapter 41 the guide brings Ezekiel into the sanctuary itself. The walls are paneled in wood and carved from floor to ceiling with cherubim and palm trees, each cherub with two faces, a human face turned toward one palm and a lion's face toward the other (Ezekiel 41:18–19). It sounds like a garden, an echo of Eden where cherubim once stood guard. The guide steps alone into the innermost room, measures it, and says, "This is the Most Holy Place" (Ezekiel 41:4). In the whole of this chapter, he speaks only one other time.

That second time comes as the prophet stands in the main hall, just outside the holiest room. There is a piece of furniture there, made entirely of wood, and the guide stops to name it.

"There was a wooden altar three cubits high and two cubits square; its corners, its base and its sides were of wood. The man said to me, 'This is the table that is before the LORD.'" (Ezekiel 41:22)

Ezekiel describes it with the ordinary Hebrew word for an altar, mizbeach, a place of offering. The guide, though, calls it a shulchan, the everyday word for a table, the kind a family gathers around to eat. Scholars debate exactly which piece of furniture this is. Many think it corresponds to the table in the old tabernacle that held the bread of the Presence, twelve loaves set out continually before God (Exodus 25:30). The Hebrew name for that bread is lechem panim, literally "bread of the face," bread laid out in God's own sight. Whatever its precise identity, the guide chose the homely word. Out of everything in that great sanctuary, the one object he troubled to explain was a table.

One way to read this is that God placed a meal at the center of his holiness. The Most Holy Place was so sacred that even the prophet waited at the doorway, yet a few steps from it stood a wooden table, close enough to share the same air. The design suggests that the God who is utterly holy also wants to be near, and that the way he chose to picture nearness was the picture every human family understands: people seated together, food between them, faces turned toward each other.

The rest of Scripture keeps setting that same table. David, hunted and weary, sang, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies" (Psalm 23:5). On the night before he died, Jesus took bread at a table with his friends and said, "This is my body given for you" (Luke 22:19), and Paul would later call that meal "the Lord's table" (1 Corinthians 10:21). At the very end of the Bible, the risen Christ describes his longing in the simplest terms imaginable: "Here I am! I stand at the door and knock. If anyone hears my voice and opens the door, I will come in and eat with that person, and they with me" (Revelation 3:20). From Ezekiel's wooden table to the upper room, God keeps choosing to show his love over a meal.

Filipinos understand this in our bones. In our homes, the first words to a visitor are rarely about business. We say "Kain tayo," let's eat, and we mean it even when the pot is small. A lola will quietly add water to the sinigang so that the unexpected cousin can have a bowl. We know that sitting down together says something words cannot, that the guest belongs and is welcome to stay a while. Ezekiel's vision tells us that this instinct reflects something true about God himself. In the heart of God's house, the furniture is arranged for company.

That has a word for anyone who feels like an exile today. Perhaps you are far from home working abroad, or far from the faith you once held warmly, or simply tired in a way that makes you feel distant from God. Ezekiel's first readers felt all of that, and God answered their distance with a table set before his face. You do not have to earn your seat by being strong. The same Lord who prepared a table for a hunted David prepares one for you, and he is glad when you come and sit.

It also has a word for how we treat one another. Dorothy Day's insight was that the love of God and the love of neighbor meet in the breaking of bread. Holiness, in Ezekiel's temple, was built around a place of fellowship, which suggests our own holiness will often look like an open table. Many of us carry a quiet loneliness, and many more sit next to someone who does. A shared meal is one of the plainest and most powerful ways to tell a person they are seen.

This week, consider setting one extra place. Invite the officemate who always eats alone, the widowed neighbor, the young family new to your church, or the relative you have drifted from, and keep the menu simple so that the company matters most. Before you eat, take a moment to remember that you are also a guest, seated by grace at a table before the Lord. When you pass the rice to someone who needed a welcome, you will be living out the picture God carved into the center of his house: a holy God who makes room, and a people who learn from him to do the same.

articles.title: Seed in Weeping Hands
articles.dek: Psalm 126 pictures a farmer crying as he walks into his field, still carrying seed. The psalm promises that the same person who goes out in tears will come home singing.
articles.quote: The tears and the seed can travel in the same hands, and God promises to bring both of them home as a harvest.
articles.body:
On June 5, 1977, a Kenyan biologist named Wangari Maathai and a small group of women planted seven trees in Kamukunji Park in Nairobi. It was World Environment Day, and the ceremony was simple enough to go almost unnoticed. Maathai had grown up in the highlands of central Kenya, where as a girl she fetched water for her mother from a clear stream near their home. Years later she remembered playing among the arrowroot leaves at its edge and trying to scoop up strands of frog eggs, thinking they were beads. By the time she was a grown woman, that stream had dried up. The forests above it had been cleared, the soil was washing away, and the rural women she spoke with kept telling her the same thing: they had no firewood, no clean water, and too little food.

Her answer was to plant trees, and to pay poor women a small sum for every seedling that survived. The work was slow and often painful. In those same years Maathai went through a public and humiliating divorce, lost her university position, and was later beaten and jailed for standing against powerful men who wanted to sell off public land. Many seedlings died. Many people laughed. But the women kept planting, and the Green Belt Movement grew until it had planted tens of millions of trees across Kenya. In 2004 Maathai became the first African woman to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Somewhere in the long middle of that story are thousands of mornings when a tired woman walked out to a bare hillside with a seedling in her hands and no proof yet that any of it would matter.

An ancient Hebrew song describes that walk exactly. Psalm 126 belongs to a small collection in the Bible called the Songs of Ascents (Psalms 120 to 134), which pilgrims sang as they climbed the roads up to Jerusalem for the great festivals. Most scholars connect this psalm with the years after the exile, when the Jewish people came home from Babylon. The first three verses look back on that homecoming with wonder: "When the LORD restored the fortunes of Zion, we were like those who dreamed. Our mouths were filled with laughter, our tongues with songs of joy" (Psalm 126:1–2). The return had felt too good to be true, like waking inside a dream.

Then the song turns to prayer, and its tone grows tender. Coming home had been wonderful, but the land was still poor. Jerusalem's walls lay in ruins, harvests were thin, and the people who had returned faced years of hard rebuilding. So the singers ask God to do it again: "Restore our fortunes, LORD, like streams in the Negev" (Psalm 126:4). The Negev is the dry southern desert of Israel. For most of the year its riverbeds, called wadis, are cracked channels of sand and stone. Then the winter rains fall in the hills, and almost overnight those dead channels fill with rushing water, and green shoots appear along the banks. The prayer asks for that kind of sudden mercy, the kind that makes a dry place run with water again.

Right after that prayer comes the picture at the heart of the psalm:

"Those who sow with tears will reap with songs of joy. Those who go out weeping, carrying seed to sow, will return with songs of joy, carrying sheaves with them." (Psalm 126:5–6)

To feel why a farmer would weep while sowing, it helps to know how farming worked in ancient Israel. Seed grain came from the last harvest. In a lean year, the barley a family set aside for planting was barley they could have eaten. Every handful thrown onto the field was bread taken off the table, buried in the ground on the hope of rain that might never come. A farmer could walk out in the morning with a hungry household behind him and a bag of seed on his shoulder, and cry the whole way to his field. He was planting because he trusted God, and he was crying because trusting God still cost him something real.

The Hebrew of verse 6 carries something English struggles to hold. The verse literally reads, "Going, he goes and weeps, carrying the bag of seed; coming, he will come with a shout of joy, carrying his sheaves." Hebrew often doubles a verb like this (halokh yelekh, "going he goes," and bo yavo, "coming he will come") to make it emphatic and certain. The psalm uses the same doubled form for both halves of the journey. The going out is certain, and the coming home is just as certain. The song gives the return the same grammatical weight as the tears.

One way to read this is as a promise about who comes home. The same person who walked out weeping is the one who walks back singing. The psalm keeps both scenes in a single life. It does not imagine one group of people who suffer and another group who celebrate. It pictures one farmer, one field, one season, and the hands that carried seed in sorrow are the same hands that carry sheaves in joy.

There is also a gentle detail in the weeping farmer's hands. He is still carrying seed. His grief has not made him put the bag down. The psalm never asks him to stop crying before he plants, and it never treats his tears as a sign of weak faith. It simply shows a man doing the next faithful thing while his heart hurts. The tears and the seed can travel in the same hands, and God promises to bring both of them home as a harvest.

The rest of Scripture echoes this. Jesus said, "unless a kernel of wheat falls to the ground and dies, it remains only a single seed. But if it dies, it produces many seeds" (John 12:24). The apostle Paul wrote to tired believers, "Let us not become weary in doing good, for at the proper time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up" (Galatians 6:9). Both passages describe the same field as Psalm 126, where the planting is costly, the waiting is long, and the harvest belongs to God's timing.

Many of us are in the sowing season right now. Perhaps you are a parent praying for a child who has wandered, and you keep setting a plate for them at Sunday lunch. Perhaps you are working abroad, sending money home to a family whose faces you see mostly on a phone screen, and some nights the loneliness is heavy. Perhaps you are caring for a sick parent, or rebuilding a marriage slowly, or serving in a small church where the results seem thin. Every one of these is a bag of seed carried by someone who is tired and sometimes crying.

Filipino farmers understand this rhythm in their bodies. Anyone who has watched a family bend over a flooded paddy during tanim, pressing young rice seedlings into the mud one by one, knows that planting is backbreaking and that the harvest is months away. The planters cannot see the golden field yet. They trust the season, and they keep their backs bent over the water.

Psalm 126 invites you to keep walking to your field. You may still be grieving, and that is allowed. Choose one small seed to put into the ground this week, even with wet eyes: a patient message to the child who has gone quiet, a prayer prayed again for the person you have nearly given up on, an hour of service you could easily skip, a kind word to the coworker who has made your life hard. These things may feel small and costly, the way a handful of barley felt to a hungry farmer. In God's hands they are seed.

Wangari Maathai did not live to see every tree she planted grow to full height, but children now play in the shade of forests that began as seedlings carried by women with sore backs and heavy hearts. The God who fills the dry wadis of the Negev with sudden water sees every seed you carry and every tear that falls on the path. Keep sowing. The same psalm that gives you permission to weep also gives you a promise to hold onto: "Those who sow with tears will reap with songs of joy" (Psalm 126:5).

articles.title: What the Elephants Know About Comfort
articles.dek: Proverbs warns that a cheerful song can hurt a grieving heart. Elephants in Thailand, and Jesus at a graveside, show us what comfort looks like instead.
articles.quote: Comfort that heals begins by coming close to the pain, and only later, when the heart is ready, does it begin to sing.
articles.body:
In the hills of northern Thailand, near the place where Thailand, Laos, and Myanmar meet, a scientist named Joshua Plotnik spent about a year watching a group of Asian elephants. Working with the primatologist Frans de Waal, he wanted to answer a simple question: what do elephants do when one of their own is upset? A frightened elephant is easy to recognize. Its ears flare wide, its tail goes stiff, and it often gives a low, anxious rumble or a sudden trumpet when something has startled it, such as a snake in the grass or a barking dog.

What happened next surprised the researchers. Nearby elephants walked over and stood close to the frightened one. They made soft, high-pitched chirping sounds, a noise the team rarely heard at other times. They reached out with their trunks and gently touched the upset elephant's face, and often they placed the tip of the trunk inside its mouth, which for an elephant is a gesture of deep trust, something like putting your hand into another person's hand. Sometimes the whole group closed in around the distressed animal in a tight, protective circle. The study, published in 2014, gave some of the clearest evidence yet that elephants console one another, and what stands out is how carefully the comforters fit themselves to the one who was hurting. They came near, they softened their voices, and they stayed.

Nearly three thousand years earlier, a collector of wisdom in Jerusalem made the same observation about people, though he came at it from the other side. He described what comfort looks like when it goes wrong.

The sayings in Proverbs 25 come with a little note at the top: "These are more proverbs of Solomon, compiled by the men of Hezekiah king of Judah" (Proverbs 25:1). Around 700 BC, royal scribes in King Hezekiah's court gathered and copied Solomon's older wisdom so it would not be lost. In this section they placed a small cluster of sayings side by side, and they share a theme. Honey is a gift, yet the scribes write, "If you find honey, eat just enough," because "too much of it, and you will vomit" (Proverbs 25:16). Visiting a neighbor is a kindness, yet "Seldom set foot in your neighbor's house" (Proverbs 25:17), because even good company can wear out its welcome. Verses 18 and 19 describe a false witness and an unreliable friend. Then comes the sharpest picture of all.

"Like one who takes away a garment on a cold day, or like vinegar poured on a wound, is one who sings songs to a heavy heart." (Proverbs 25:20)

Each image would have stung an ancient Israelite. Nights in the hill country of Judah can be bitterly cold, and for a poor family the outer cloak doubled as a blanket. The law of Moses protected it fiercely: "If you take your neighbor's cloak as a pledge, return it by sunset, because that cloak is the only covering your neighbor has. What else can they sleep in?" (Exodus 22:26–27). To pull that cloak off someone on a cold day was to leave them shivering exactly when they needed warmth most.

The second image has a fascinating backstory in Hebrew. The original text speaks of chomets (vinegar) poured on neter, a word for natron, a natural mineral soda that people used for washing. The same word appears in Jeremiah 2:22 for a cleansing agent. Pour vinegar on soda and it hisses, foams, and boils over, which is why older English versions read "vinegar upon nitre." The NIV follows the ancient Greek translation and says "wound," which makes the pain more personal. Either way the picture is the same: something that should be harmless produces a violent reaction because it meets the wrong thing at the wrong time.

The phrase "heavy heart" translates the Hebrew lev ra, literally "a bad heart," meaning a heart that is troubled or grieving. It is close to the expression King Artaxerxes used when he looked at Nehemiah's face and said, "This can be nothing but sadness of heart" (Nehemiah 2:2). The person who sings to such a heart is probably trying to help. Songs are good, as honey is good and visits are good. The whole cluster of proverbs teaches that a good thing offered in the wrong measure or the wrong moment can wound, and comfort depends on fit. The elephants seemed to understand this by instinct. Their chirps were soft and their bodies came close, so that the help matched the need.

Filipinos are among the most cheerful people on earth, and that resilience is a genuine gift from God. We laugh through floods and joke at wakes. Yet our cheer can sometimes become the song sung to a heavy heart. Someone tells us their marriage is struggling, and we answer, "Kaya mo 'yan!" A friend loses a job, and we say, "Smile ka lang, God has a reason." A mother miscarries, and someone tells her, "At least you can try again." Every one of those lines may be true and well meant, and every one can feel like a cloak pulled away on a cold night. Paul gives the better way plainly: "Rejoice with those who rejoice; mourn with those who mourn" (Romans 12:15).

Job's three friends are a sobering example. When they first arrived, "they sat on the ground with him for seven days and seven nights. No one said a word to him, because they saw how great his suffering was" (Job 2:13). Those seven silent days were the best thing they ever did for him. Their trouble began when they opened their mouths and started explaining his pain.

The gospel shows us God's own way of comforting, and it looks remarkably like those elephants in the Thai hills. When Jesus arrived at the tomb of his friend Lazarus, he already knew that within minutes he would call Lazarus out alive. He held the most hopeful news anyone has ever carried to a funeral. Yet when he saw Mary weeping, John tells us "he was deeply moved in spirit and troubled" (John 11:33), and then, in the shortest verse in the Bible, "Jesus wept" (John 11:35). He came close to the grief and entered it before he spoke the word that ended it.

That scene captures the whole story of salvation. God did not shout encouragement at a broken world from a safe distance. He came near in Jesus, who was "a man of suffering, and familiar with pain" (Isaiah 53:3). Because of that, the writer of Hebrews can say, "we do not have a high priest who is unable to empathize with our weaknesses" (Hebrews 4:15). Comfort that heals begins by coming close to the pain, and only later, when the heart is ready, does it begin to sing. The songs do come. Scripture promises that "weeping may stay for the night, but rejoicing comes in the morning" (Psalm 30:5), and there is "a time to weep and a time to laugh" (Ecclesiastes 3:4). Wisdom lies in knowing which hour it is.

Perhaps someone in your life is carrying a heavy heart right now: a coworker, a cousin, a friend who has gone quiet in the group chat. This week you could go to them and say less than you planned, perhaps asking, "Do you want to talk about it, or should I just sit with you for a while?" A hand on the shoulder, a meal left at the door, or an hour of patient listening may do more than any verse quoted too soon. Keep the encouraging words ready, and let love tell you when it is time to speak them.

And if you are the one with the heavy heart today, take comfort in this. Jesus does not stand at a distance singing cheerful songs at you. He comes close, he understands, and he weeps with you, and in his time he will turn your night into morning.
